power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

codebook_check.title: Codebook Check
codebook_check.summary_text:
-  We parsed 30 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
-  1 of 254 data columns (0%) is documented in a codebook; 253 are not.
-  A codebook was found and parsed (30 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents `Technology characteristics`, `Accuracy and errors`, `Ease of use` while the data has `logical_run_id`, `run_id`, `settled_responses`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

table.label: Export machinery / paradata column (not a measured variable).

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 50 codebook/README/label sources and 254 data columns across 20 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (30 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents `Technology characteristics`, `Accuracy and errors`, `Ease of use` while the data has `logical_run_id`, `run_id`, `settled_responses`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

#### README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including 'README' in the name of your overview document.

#### Archive Files

The following files are not ZIP archives: screening_decisions.csv.gz, original_runs_decisions.csv.gz. We recommend the `.zip` format for archives: only ZIP stores its file listing in a way that lets a tool inspect the contents without downloading the whole archive, so a `.zip` is more discoverable and re-usable than a `.7z`, `.rar`, `.tar` or `.tar.gz`.

#### Unclassified Files

We could not classify 39 files by name or extension: screening_decisions.csv.gz, original_runs_decisions.csv.gz, .env.example, Makefile, .gitattributes, Evaluation HTML Files.zip, .dockerignore, Dockerfile, lrec.properties, application.properties. #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 103 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (103). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 254 columns across 20 data files.
#### Issues Identified
2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 20 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

**`os.chdir()` in the code**
**2 scripts call `os.chdir()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with `pass`. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring an `os.chdir()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("tests/test_code_provenance.py", "qualframe_multiverse-prep_595c937.zip/tests/test_code_provenance.py"
), "os.chdir() removed" = c(1L, 1L), "Path(s) it set" = c("(non-literal)", 
"(non-literal)")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

#### Reported vs. reproduced
8 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 0 matched (0 fully, 0 partially) — 0% found.
Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The "Plausible" column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output's own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

#### Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)
7 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook files bundle the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the files itself, with nothing re-run. We extracted 81 result tables (36 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.

info.title: The analytic multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis: a framework, open tools, and a screening study

author.affiliation:
Department of Family Medicine
								University of Ottawa
								
									Ottawa
									Ontario
									Canada

text.text: Background.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to apply predefined codebooks to qualitative data, and studies of this practice usually report agreement with human coding for a single configuration.

However, each configuration rests on many defensible choices (e.g., how the task is worded, how the codebook is presented, and how agreement is scored), and the extent to which results depend on these choices remains relatively unknown.
Methods.

I describe the analytic multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis (i.e., the set of defensible configurations for producing and scoring codes), define what a multiverse study should report, propose a staged design for exploring it, and release two open-source tools, QualFrame and QualBench, that record each choice as a setting and score every run.

In a screening study, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna coded 40 open-access smoking-cessation trial reports for 94 behaviour change techniques under a half-fraction factorial design that varied task instructions, codebook division, reasoning effort, instruction wording, and code order, with repeat runs of one configuration.
Agreement with historical Human Behaviour-Change Project annotations was measured with the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC).
Exploratory analyses examined majority votes and earlier runs of four models on 50 reports excluded from screening.
Results.
Across 32 configurations (38 runs; recorded API spend US$13.66), MCC ranged from 0.24 to 0.57.
Four runs of one configuration varied by at most 0.02 in MCC; however, of the codes applied by at least one of these runs, 43% to 64% were not applied by all four.

Within this design, the contrasts for task instructions, reasoning effort, and codebook division each exceeded the average difference between the two models, and their effects depended on one another and on the model; for example, asking the model to decide on every code raised MCC by 0.10 with the whole codebook but by 0.02 with the codebook divided.

The apparent cost of dividing the codebook fell from 0.045 to 0.011 when scoring was restricted to the 12 techniques the annotators prioritized, and balanced accuracy ranked a different configuration best.
Earlier runs of four models with similar agreement on the screening reports diverged on the 50 excluded reports, where their majority vote had agreement similar to the best model.
Agreement with a reference depended on configuration choices, their interactions, the scoring scope, and the reports scored.
Studies of AI-assisted coding should report the configurations they explored and test whether their conclusions survive these choices.
To build a cumulative evidence base, I propose a research agenda that others can take up independently with the open tools and a common reporting format.

Large language models (LLMs; i.e., models trained on large bodies of text to generate and classify language) can now apply a qualitative codebook to interviews, documents, and open-text responses far faster than a human team.

A growing literature reports how well they do so, from early demonstrations of deductive coding (Xiao et al., 2023; Chew et al., 2023; Tai et al., 2024) to larger evaluations against expert coders (Dunivin, 2025; Than et al., 2025) and applications in health and implementation research (Turner et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A growing literature reports how well they do so, from early demonstrations of deductive coding <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Xiao et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Chew et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Tai et al., 2024)</ref> to larger evaluations against expert coders <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Dunivin, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Than et al., 2025)</ref> and applications in health and implementation research <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Turner et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Reviews written for health researchers now weigh the promise of these methods against their pitfalls (Cook et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Reviews written for health researchers now weigh the promise of these methods against their pitfalls <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cook et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, most of these studies report one configuration (i.e., the full set of choices used to produce and score the codes) and its agreement with human coding.

A configuration is a stack of decisions: how long documents are divided, how the codebook is presented, how the task is worded, which model and settings are used, how invalid outputs are handled, and how agreement is counted.
Few of these decisions have a single correct answer, and most are made once and left untested.

For example, in a review of 27 papers in leading social science journals that used LLMs as measurement instruments, prompt and model choices were usually justified by intuition or reputation, and only four papers reported how answers were extracted from model output (Desai et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For example, in a review of 27 papers in leading social science journals that used LLMs as measurement instruments, prompt and model choices were usually justified by intuition or reputation, and only four papers reported how answers were extracted from model output <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Desai et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: There is good evidence that such decisions matter.
Meaning-preserving changes to prompt formatting moved accuracy by up to 76 points, and the best format for one model was a poor guide to another (Sclar et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Meaning-preserving changes to prompt formatting moved accuracy by up to 76 points, and the best format for one model was a poor guide to another <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Sclar et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In another example, Baumann et al. (2025) re-ran 37 annotation tasks from 21 published studies with 18 models and found that configuration choices led to incorrect conclusions for about a third of hypotheses, even with state-of-the-art models, and that a handful of prompt rewordings could make almost any result appear statistically significant.
text.formatted: In another example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Baumann et al. (2025)</ref> re-ran 37 annotation tasks from 21 published studies with 18 models and found that configuration choices led to incorrect conclusions for about a third of hypotheses, even with state-of-the-art models, and that a handful of prompt rewordings could make almost any result appear statistically significant.

text.text: Further, in Messing's (2026) decomposition of LLM evaluation pipelines, ignoring the variance contributed by prompts, judges, and temperature made standard errors 40-60% too small.
text.formatted: Further, in <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Messing's (2026)</ref> decomposition of LLM evaluation pipelines, ignoring the variance contributed by prompts, judges, and temperature made standard errors 40-60% too small.

text.text: Work on qualitative coding itself has begun to test individual choices, including temperature and agent persona (Borchers et al., 2026), uniform versus code-specific prompts (Rodríguez-Triana et al., 2026), prompt stability (Barrie et al., 2024), and the biases that models introduce (Ashwin et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Work on qualitative coding itself has begun to test individual choices, including temperature and agent persona <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Borchers et al., 2026)</ref>, uniform versus code-specific prompts <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Rodríguez-Triana et al., 2026)</ref>, prompt stability <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Barrie et al., 2024)</ref>, and the biases that models introduce <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ashwin et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, these studies typically vary one or two choices on one dataset, and others question whether agreement with human coders measures the quality of coding at all (Liu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, these studies typically vary one or two choices on one dataset, and others question whether agreement with human coders measures the quality of coding at all <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Liu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, simple questions such as 'how much does agreement with human coding depend on the configuration?' and 'which configuration choices matter most?' do not yet have robust answers.
These questions have practical consequences.

Reviewers can fairly ask whether a team simply kept the configuration that happened to work; models are updated and retired, so a result tied to one exact configuration may not be repeatable a year later (Chen et al., 2024); and teams with small budgets need to know where extra spending buys agreement and where it buys nothing.
text.formatted: Reviewers can fairly ask whether a team simply kept the configuration that happened to work; models are updated and retired, so a result tied to one exact configuration may not be repeatable a year later <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chen et al., 2024)</ref>; and teams with small budgets need to know where extra spending buys agreement and where it buys nothing.

text.text: Prompts, model identifiers, task scope, and scoring rules should be reported for transparency whatever their effects, but knowing which choices matter most would show where sensitivity analyses are most needed.
Psychology encountered a similar problem, described as the 'garden of forking paths' (Gelman & Loken, 2013), in which flexible analytic choices can produce almost any result.
text.formatted: Psychology encountered a similar problem, described as the 'garden of forking paths' <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gelman & Loken, 2013)</ref>, in which flexible analytic choices can produce almost any result.

text.text: Its response was to run every defensible analysis and report the spread, through multiverse analysis (i.e., reporting results across all reasonable combinations of analytic choices; Steegen et al., 2016), specification curve analysis (i.e., plotting every specification's result together with the choices behind it; Simonsohn et al., 2020), and many-analysts studies (i.e., independent teams analyzing the same data; Silberzahn et al., 2018). Bell et al. (2022) adapted this reasoning to machine learning research, distinguishing the exploration of a space of configurations to support robust conclusions from optimization within it.
text.formatted: Its response was to run every defensible analysis and report the spread, through multiverse analysis (i.e., reporting results across all reasonable combinations of analytic choices; <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Steegen et al., 2016)</ref>, specification curve analysis (i.e., plotting every specification's result together with the choices behind it; <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Simonsohn et al., 2020)</ref>, and many-analysts studies (i.e., independent teams analyzing the same data; <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Silberzahn et al., 2018)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bell et al. (2022)</ref> adapted this reasoning to machine learning research, distinguishing the exploration of a space of configurations to support robust conclusions from optimization within it.

text.text: Health research has a parallel tradition of screening many intervention components in efficient factorial experiments before testing the most promising in full (Collins, 2018).
text.formatted: Health research has a parallel tradition of screening many intervention components in efficient factorial experiments before testing the most promising in full <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Collins, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Here, I adapt these ideas to AI-assisted directed content analysis (i.e., the deductive form of qualitative content analysis in which coders apply codes defined in advance from a framework or theory; Hsieh & Shannon, 2005).
text.formatted: Here, I adapt these ideas to AI-assisted directed content analysis (i.e., the deductive form of qualitative content analysis in which coders apply codes defined in advance from a framework or theory; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hsieh & Shannon, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: To this end, the paper pursues two aims.

The first is robustness, that is, identifying which conclusions about AI-assisted coding survive reasonable analytic choices; the second is optimization, or identifying which configuration gives useful agreement at an acceptable cost.
A multiverse study serves the first aim before the second; it is not a search for a winning prompt.

Specifically, I 1) set out a framework for the analytic multiverse of AI-assisted coding in two layers, together with the quantities a multiverse study should report and a staged design for exploring it (Section 2); 2) describe two open-source tools that make each choice a recorded setting and score every run (Section 3); 3) report a first screening study on a public dataset, including exploratory analyses of combining runs and of reports excluded from screening (Sections 3 and 4); and 4) discuss implications for practice and reporting, and propose a research agenda that others can take up independently (Section 5).

The empirical study evaluates the application of a fixed codebook and the reproducibility of report-level coding decisions; it does not evaluate category development, interpretive depth, or the adequacy of a final qualitative account.
Before AI-assisted coding can be relied on as a research instrument, we must establish how much its results depend on the choices made in configuring it.
An AI coding result is one path through two layers of choices: those that produce the codes and those that score them.
Following Steegen et al. (2016), I refer to the set of paths that a careful analyst could defend as the analytic multiverse.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Steegen et al. (2016)</ref>, I refer to the set of paths that a careful analyst could defend as the analytic multiverse.

text.text: In directed content analysis, coders apply codes defined in advance to units of text.
When an LLM does the coding, the unit of evaluation is usually a document × code pair (i.e., whether the code was applied to the document) and, where the model cites evidence, a passage.
Table 1 lists the forks considered here, and Figure 1 shows nine of them as a map of possible paths.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> lists the forks considered here, and Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref> shows nine of them as a map of possible paths.

text.text: The first layer contains the choices that produce codes (e.g., how the codebook is presented and which model is used); the second contains the choices that turn codes into an agreement score (e.g., the reference and the statistic).
Note.

The row 'Documents scored' was added after the screening study reported here, in which the ranking of models changed between the screening reports and the reports excluded from screening (Section 4.9).
Every AI coding result is one path through many choices.
Nine of the forks in Table 1 are shown in the two layers of producing and scoring codes, each with three example options; the highlighted boxes trace one possible path.
text.formatted: Nine of the forks in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> are shown in the two layers of producing and scoring codes, each with three example options; the highlighted boxes trace one possible path.

text.text: Three options at each of nine forks give 19,683 possible paths.
Most studies report one path; a multiverse study runs many and reports the spread.
I treat a configuration as defensible when it is compatible with the intended coding task, preserves the constructs the codebook defines, and could plausibly be used in a real research workflow.
Importantly, the two layers also differ in kind.

Forks that produce codes change how a fixed task is implemented, whereas several scoring forks change the evaluation target itself (e.g., which reference is used, which codes or document sections are eligible, and how sensitivity is weighed against specificity).
A conclusion that changes with such a fork may therefore reflect a different question rather than a lack of robustness.
Some forks are the questions a study wants answered, such as whether presenting one codebook section at a time improves agreement.
I call these design factors and estimate their effects.

Others have no principled answer, such as the exact wording of an instruction or the order in which codes are listed; I call these incidental choices and vary them deliberately, so that conclusions do not hinge on one arbitrary version.
Their effects are not of interest in themselves; rather, the variance they contribute is part of the uncertainty of any conclusion about the design factors.
The distinction mirrors the fixed and random facets of generalizability theory; for example, Messing (2026) treats prompt variants as random and models as fixed.
The same configuration run twice can produce different codes.

Before any choice is credited with an improvement, a study should therefore repeat at least one configuration and estimate how much agreement varies by chance alone, which I refer to as the noise floor.
Two quantities are worth reporting: the spread of summary agreement across repeats, and agreement between repeats at the level of individual document × code decisions.
These can diverge, because errors in opposite directions cancel in a summary statistic.
Said another way, two runs can reach the same agreement score while disagreeing about which codes apply.
Agreement requires a reference, ideally independent coding by trained people.
However, references differ in quality and scope: a single coder or an adjudicated consensus, a historical annotation project with its own rules, or an earlier model-assisted coding.
Agreement with a reference therefore measures concordance with one careful reading rather than truth.
Prevalence (i.e., the proportion of units in which a code is present) also shapes what agreement means, and the common statistics express different objectives.

F1 ignores true negatives, whereas balanced accuracy weighs sensitivity and specificity equally, so that when codes are rare it rewards finding annotated codes even at the cost of many false positives.

The Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), or the correlation between the coded and reference decisions (ranging from -1 to 1, where 0 indicates chance agreement), uses all four cells of the confusion matrix (Chicco & Jurman, 2020).
text.formatted: The Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), or the correlation between the coded and reference decisions (ranging from -1 to 1, where 0 indicates chance agreement), uses all four cells of the confusion matrix <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chicco & Jurman, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The primary statistic should be chosen before results are seen, and rules that read nothing (e.g., marking every code absent) reported alongside it.
Finally, whether units the reference never assessed should count as absences is an evaluation assumption rather than a fact about the data; I describe such units as 'not annotated'.

I recommend that a multiverse study report six quantities: 1) the noise floor, or the variation in agreement across repeats of one configuration; 2) the specification curve, which shows every configuration's agreement, sorted, with the choices behind each configuration marked underneath (Simonsohn et al., 2020); 3) the variance decomposition, or the share of the spread attributable to each factor and interaction (Messing, 2026); 4) the cost-agreement frontier, which identifies the configurations that give the most agreement for each budget; 5) code-level robustness, or how far agreement for each code holds across the multiverse; and 6) rank stability, or whether the ordering of models or configurations survives changes to the other forks, including the scoring choices and the documents scored.
text.formatted: I recommend that a multiverse study report six quantities: 1) the noise floor, or the variation in agreement across repeats of one configuration; 2) the specification curve, which shows every configuration's agreement, sorted, with the choices behind each configuration marked underneath <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Simonsohn et al., 2020)</ref>; 3) the variance decomposition, or the share of the spread attributable to each factor and interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Messing, 2026)</ref>; 4) the cost-agreement frontier, which identifies the configurations that give the most agreement for each budget; 5) code-level robustness, or how far agreement for each code holds across the multiverse; and 6) rank stability, or whether the ordering of models or configurations survives changes to the other forks, including the scoring choices and the documents scored.

text.text: Taken together, these quantities describe how much a reported result depends on the path taken.
The full multiverse is too large to run; three options at each of nine forks already give 19,683 configurations per dataset.

I therefore propose exploring it in stages, spending more only where an earlier stage shows that it is worthwhile (Figure 2), much as the multiphase optimization strategy screens candidate intervention components in efficient factorial experiments before evaluating the most promising (Collins, 2018).
text.formatted: I therefore propose exploring it in stages, spending more only where an earlier stage shows that it is worthwhile (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>), much as the multiphase optimization strategy screens candidate intervention components in efficient factorial experiments before evaluating the most promising <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Collins, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A study begins by declaring the multiverse (i.e., the forks, their levels, which are design factors and which are incidental, and any paths excluded as indefensible) and freezing the declaration before any run, which limits researcher degrees of freedom.
It then measures the noise floor and screens many factors in a fractional factorial design (i.e., a planned subset of all factor combinations) using inexpensive models.

The focus stage crosses the factors that matter in a full factorial design with stronger models, because changing one factor at a time cannot detect an interaction, and confirmation tests the selected configurations on other datasets, documents, or codes.

Throughout, every run is rescored under each scoring choice without further model calls, and every configuration is reported, not only the best, because selecting the best of many runs inflates expected performance (Messing, 2026).
text.formatted: Throughout, every run is rescored under each scoring choice without further model calls, and every configuration is reported, not only the best, because selecting the best of many runs inflates expected performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Messing, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: QualFrame applies a codebook to a set of documents through a model provider's application programming interface (API), and QualBench scores the resulting codes against a reference.
Both are open source (MIT licence), written in Python, and archived on Zenodo (van Allen, 2026).
For each run, QualFrame locks the configuration, saves the model settings, prompts, codebook, and a hash of every input, and records every request with its token use and cost.
Several forks in Table 1, such as the instruction package, the division of the codebook into parts, the model, and the reasoning effort, are settings.
text.formatted: Several forks in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, such as the instruction package, the division of the codebook into parts, the model, and the reasoning effort, are settings.

text.text: Importantly, the reference never enters QualFrame; only QualBench uses it, so the same outputs can be rescored under any scoring choice without further model calls.

For this study, I developed a screening runner (with AI assistance; see Declarations) that expands a declared multiverse into one locked configuration per run and enforces spending limits (Supplementary Section S1).

The Human Behaviour-Change Project (HBCP) released an open-access corpus of published smokingcessation intervention reports annotated with behaviour change techniques (BCTs; i.e., observable, replicable components of interventions designed to change behaviour; Michie et al., 2013), as described by Michie et al. (2017) and Bonin et al. (2020).
text.formatted: The Human Behaviour-Change Project (HBCP) released an open-access corpus of published smokingcessation intervention reports annotated with behaviour change techniques (BCTs; i.e., observable, replicable components of interventions designed to change behaviour; <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Michie et al., 2013)</ref>, as described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Michie et al. (2017)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bonin et al. (2020)</ref>.

text.text: I used the 95 reports with BCT annotations and the 94 van Allen • The multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis codes those annotations use: the 93 techniques of the BCT Taxonomy v1 (Michie et al., 2013) and 'Advise to change behaviour'.
text.formatted: I used the 95 reports with BCT annotations and the 94 van Allen • The multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis codes those annotations use: the 93 techniques of the BCT Taxonomy v1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Michie et al., 2013)</ref> and 'Advise to change behaviour'.

text.text: Code labels and definitions were taken from the BCT Ontology (Marques et al., 2024), and the codes fall into 16 taxonomy groups.
text.formatted: Code labels and definitions were taken from the BCT Ontology <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Marques et al., 2024)</ref>, and the codes fall into 16 taxonomy groups.

text.text: The reference was the HBCP annotation export, reduced to which BCTs were annotated in each report.
About 6% of report × BCT units were annotated, with a mean of 5.7 BCTs per report.
Only 40 of the 94 codes were annotated in at least one of the 40 screening reports, so any coding of the other 54 codes in those reports counted as a false positive.
Treating units without an annotation as absences is therefore an evaluation assumption (Section 2.4).
Importantly, the coding task and the reference annotation were not identical.

HBCP annotators did not annotate Discussion sections, annotated only techniques directed at the target behaviour of the intervention, and assigned annotations to study arms (Bonin et al., 2020); the project also prioritized 12 BCTs.
text.formatted: HBCP annotators did not annotate Discussion sections, annotated only techniques directed at the target behaviour of the intervention, and assigned annotations to study arms <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bonin et al., 2020)</ref>; the project also prioritized 12 BCTs.

text.text: In contrast, the models received the full text of each report, with no restriction to the target behaviour or to particular arms.
Both sides were pooled to the report, such that a BCT was present if it was coded anywhere in the report or annotated for any arm.
A model could therefore make a defensible coding that lowered its measured agreement; for example, a technique described only in a report's Discussion section would count as a false positive.
The secondary scoring scopes described in Section 3.5 partly address this.

In earlier runs of the same pipeline, reported in a companion manuscript in preparation, four models (Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Claude Sonnet 5.5) coded all 95 reports with one configuration: the 'decide every code' instructions, the whole codebook in one request, and each model's preset reasoning effort (QualFrame 0.9.0, 13 October 2026).
Their agreement on all 95 reports (MCC 0.55 to 0.61) was known before the screen was designed; their agreement on the 50 reports later excluded from screening had not been computed.
I refer to these four runs as the original runs.
The 40 screening reports were drawn at random (seed 20261023) from the 90 reports not used in an earlier five-report pilot; the remaining 50 were not used in screening.

The unit of agreement was the report × BCT pair, giving 3,760 units per run.

A BCT was counted as applied when the run recorded at least one coding for it in the report, including codings whose quotations could not be located; explicit absences and missing decisions were counted as not applied.
The primary measure was MCC over all 94 BCTs.
Secondary measures were balanced accuracy, F1, sensitivity, precision, and the number of BCTs coded per report.

Every run was also rescored under two secondary scoring scopes: the 16 taxonomy groups, where a group was present if any of its BCTs was, and the 12 BCTs that HBCP prioritized, a scope closer to the reference's coverage.
Output compliance and cost were also recorded (Supplementary Section S1).
All configuration-level analyses weight the 32 configurations equally, with cell 09 represented by the mean of its four runs.
For the noise floor, I compared the four runs of cell 09 both in summary MCC and unit by unit.

Main effects were estimated as the difference in mean MCC between the two levels of a factor across all 32 configurations, so that each effect is averaged over the other factors and both models; two-way interactions and conditional effects were estimated in the same way, under the primary scope and both secondary scopes.
A saturated variance decomposition partitioned the variation among the 32 configurations into model, the five main effects, the ten two-way interactions, and their interactions with model.

Uncertainty about which reports were coded was estimated with a bootstrap (i.e., repeated resampling of the data with replacement) of the 40 reports, with 2,000 resamples (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993), and I report 95% percentile intervals; these do not include run-to-run variation.

text.text: This study sought to describe the analytic multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis and to explore a first part of it, using a screening design on a public dataset.
Three findings stand out.
First, choices interacted.

Within this design, the contrasts for task instructions, reasoning effort, and codebook division were each larger than the average difference between the two tested models, and the effect of each depended on the others and on the model; for example, asking the model to decide on every code helped most when the whole codebook was sent at once.
Said another way, a comparison of models at one fixed configuration answers a narrower question than it appears to.

The tested paraphrase and code shuffle changed agreement little, although one paraphrase and one shuffle are thin samples of those spaces, and meaning-preserving changes have had much larger effects elsewhere (Sclar et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The tested paraphrase and code shuffle changed agreement little, although one paraphrase and one shuffle are thin samples of those spaces, and meaning-preserving changes have had much larger effects elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Sclar et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Second, part of the variation in agreement was variation in alignment with a particular reference.

The design factors acted mainly by changing how many codes the models applied, while the reference annotated 5.7 BCTs per report under rules that excluded Discussion sections and techniques not directed at the target behaviour.

Configurations that coded more were therefore penalized partly for codings outside the reference's coverage, not only for errors, and the apparent cost of dividing the codebook shrank from -0.045 over all 94 BCTs to -0.011 on the 12 BCTs the annotators prioritized.
Majority voting worked through the same channel, bringing the number of codes per report closer to the reference's.
Agreement statistics alone cannot distinguish error from misalignment.
Third, rankings were not stable.

Ranking configurations by balanced accuracy rather than MCC selected a different best configuration, although this partly reflects a different objective, because balanced accuracy rewards the sensitivity gained by coding more.
Unfortunately, the 40 screening reports also proved a poor guide to model rankings; four models with similar agreement on them diverged on the 50 excluded reports.
In hindsight, the bootstrap intervals on the screening reports were already wide enough to warn that similar point estimates on 40 reports were weak evidence of equivalence.

Nonetheless, a vote across the four models had agreement similar to the best of them on the excluded reports without requiring the analyst to know in advance which model was best, a practical hedge when model rankings are uncertain, although it costs as much as all four runs together.
Voting across samples is an established way to make language model outputs more reliable (Wang et al., 2023); here, voting across different models helped more than voting across repeats of one model.
text.formatted: Voting across samples is an established way to make language model outputs more reliable <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Wang et al., 2023)</ref>; here, voting across different models helped more than voting across repeats of one model.

text.text: For teams using AI-assisted coding, the results suggest four practices.

First, prompts, model identifiers, settings, task scope, and scoring rules should be reported in full, and the choices with the largest contrasts here (instructions, codebook presentation, and reasoning effort) warrant sensitivity analyses.

Provider defaults are themselves choices; for example, the original Haiku run with the provider's default effort reached 0.563, whereas the cell 09 runs with low effort set explicitly averaged 0.489, although a change of software version also separates them.

Second, at least one configuration should be repeated, and unitlevel agreement between repeats reported alongside summary agreement; where individual codings are reviewed and used as evidence, the instability of individual decisions matters more than the stability of the summary.
Third, where the reference's scope differs from the coding task, results should also be reported for a scoring scope that matches the reference's coverage.

Finally, the primary agreement statistic should be chosen in advance together with the objective it represents, and a configuration or model should be chosen on some documents and confirmed on others.

For methodologists and editors, these forks are candidates for required sensitivity analyses in reporting guidance on AI-assisted qualitative analysis, and a small specification curve is now inexpensive to produce; this screen cost US$13.66 in recorded API spend.

These results extend evidence that configuration choices can change the conclusions of LLM-based annotation (Sclar et al., 2024; Baumann et al., 2025; Messing, 2026) to deductive qualitative coding with a large codebook.
text.formatted: These results extend evidence that configuration choices can change the conclusions of LLM-based annotation <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Sclar et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Baumann et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Messing, 2026)</ref> to deductive qualitative coding with a large codebook.

text.text: In this setting, the choices with the largest contrasts were structural (i.e., whether every code must be decided, and how the codebook is presented) rather than matters of wording.

A companion study applied the same tools to 17 interviews coded against 115 codes from the updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and its Outcomes Addendum (Damschroder et al., 2022a (Damschroder et al., , 2022b)), with an earlier model-assisted coding as the reference, and observed a similar pattern, in that 'decide every code' improved agreement more when the whole codebook was sent at once (manuscript in preparation; the parent study is described by Radhakrishnan et al., 2026).

text.text: Those results are not part of the evidence presented here.
This research is subject to several limitations worth noting when interpreting the findings.
First, agreement is not validity, and here the reference and the coding task differed in scope (Section 3.2).
Treating units that were not annotated as absences counts as errors some codings that a reviewer might accept, and references have their own blind spots (Liu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Treating units that were not annotated as absences counts as errors some codings that a reviewer might accept, and references have their own blind spots <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Liu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A blinded review of a stratified sample of disagreements would show how much of the measured disagreement reflects error rather than differences in scope; I did not undertake one here, and it is a priority for future work.

Second, the screen used one dataset of published English-language trial reports, which the models may have seen during training, and two low-cost models; effects for stronger models are unknown because the focus stage was not run.
Third, it used 40 reports, and model rankings on them did not hold on the reports excluded from screening.
Fourth, repeat-run variation was measured for one configuration per model, and the bootstrap intervals do not include it.
Fifth, the half fraction aliases each two-way interaction with a three-way interaction, and each incidental factor was represented by a single alternative.
Finally, the analyses of combining runs and of excluded reports were added after the screen and are exploratory, and specific models and prices will date quickly (Chen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Finally, the analyses of combining runs and of excluded reports were added after the screen and are exploratory, and specific models and prices will date quickly <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these limitations argue for treating the specific estimates reported here as hypothesis generating rather than definitive; the aim is to learn which kinds of choice matter, which should outlast any one model.
One dataset cannot establish which choices matter in general; that requires evidence from many datasets, frameworks, and kinds of text.

I therefore propose a research agenda that others can take up independently, with the aim of advancing the methodology of AI-assisted qualitative analysis rather than validating any one tool or model.

The questions I consider most pressing are 1) which forks account for most of the variation in agreement, and whether their ordering holds across datasets and frameworks; 2) whether model rankings survive changes to instructions, codebook presentation, scoring, and the documents scored; 3) which properties of a code (e.g., its prevalence, abstraction, and overlap with other codes) predict whether its agreement is robust; and 4) whether conclusions drawn from agreement hold when the quality of coding is judged directly (Liu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The questions I consider most pressing are 1) which forks account for most of the variation in agreement, and whether their ordering holds across datasets and frameworks; 2) whether model rankings survive changes to instructions, codebook presentation, scoring, and the documents scored; 3) which properties of a code (e.g., its prevalence, abstraction, and overlap with other codes) predict whether its agreement is robust; and 4) whether conclusions drawn from agreement hold when the quality of coding is judged directly <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Liu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Progress on these questions does not require a coordinated project, only studies that can be compared.

To this end, I suggest that researchers who evaluate AI-assisted coding against existing human coding declare their multiverse before running it, include at least the choices with the largest contrasts here (task instructions, codebook presentation, and reasoning effort), repeat at least one configuration, and report the six quantities in Section 2.5 together with the declaration.
QualFrame, QualBench, and the declaration and scripts used here are openly available and can be adapted to other data.
Studies reported in this way could later be combined across datasets and frameworks (Supplementary Section S5).

In a first screen of the analytic multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis, choices about task instructions, codebook presentation, and reasoning effort produced larger contrasts in agreement with historical human annotation than the difference between two models, interacted with one another and with the model, and changed which configuration looked best.
The apparent effect of one choice also depended on which annotations were treated as the reference.
Repeat runs, reports excluded from screening, more than one agreement statistic, and more than one scoring scope were each needed to see this.
General lessons will require many datasets coded by people, and comparable multiverse studies, run independently and reported in a common format, are an important first step towards them.
Before AIassisted coding can be relied on as a research instrument, we must establish how much its results depend on the choices made in configuring it.

Variance decomposition.

The variance decomposition partitioned the sum of squares of the 32 configuration MCCs into a saturated set of orthogonal contrasts (i.e., one contrast for each degree of freedom): model, the five main effects, the ten two-way interactions, and the interaction of model with each of these.
Its shares depend on the models, levels, prompts, corpus, and scoring rules chosen and are not general variance components.

I compared the decomposition with the variance expected from run-torun noise, using the pooled standard deviation of the repeat runs and assuming that run-to-run variation elsewhere in the design resembled that of cell 09.

Among the differences between models, the largest was in the effect of reasoning effort (5.2% of the variation), and the main effects of instruction wording and code order together accounted for 1.5%.

Suitable data.

Interviews, focus groups, open-text survey responses, or documents coded against a codebook or framework (e.g., the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, the Theoretical Domains Framework, a behaviour change taxonomy, or a team's own codebook) are suitable, together with the codebook as the coders used it and, ideally, each coder's independent decisions before reconciliation as well as the agreed coding.
Ethics approval and participant consent must allow the text to be processed by an AI service.
A team can install QualFrame, adapt the declaration used here or write its own, and run it on its own computers, sending text only to the AI services its approvals allow.
QualBench scores the runs locally against the team's coding, so the configuration contrasts and their uncertainty can be reported without sharing raw text.

Beyond its contribution to the agenda, such a study gives a team a benchmark of how AI coding compares with its own coding, code by code, and of which configurations worked best for its data and at what cost.

Studies that report comparable contrasts with their uncertainty could later be combined in a hierarchical meta-analysis, with datasets as the unit of replication and frameworks kept distinct, because codes from different frameworks are not common categories.

Where unit-level decisions are available, agreement at the level of document × code decisions can also be modelled with fixed effects for design factors, random effects for incidental choices, and random effects for documents and codes nested within datasets, following Messing (2026); such a model yields variance shares for each factor and interaction, and indicates whether additional prompt variants, repeats, or documents would most reduce uncertainty.
text.formatted: Where unit-level decisions are available, agreement at the level of document × code decisions can also be modelled with fixed effects for design factors, random effects for incidental choices, and random effects for documents and codes nested within datasets, following <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Messing (2026)</ref>; such a model yields variance shares for each factor and interaction, and indicates whether additional prompt variants, repeats, or documents would most reduce uncertainty.

text.text: Imagine that several research teams, each holding interviews or documents already coded against a different framework, independently run comparable multiverses on their own data and report the same contrasts.

If the advantage of deciding on every code held across datasets and frameworks, this would suggest a general property of how current models apply codebooks, and could inform default settings in tools and reporting guidance.

If instead the best configuration varied by framework or by kind of text, this would suggest that configurations should be tuned and confirmed for each project, and that reporting guidance should require such confirmation.

QualBench measures.

At the level of document × code units, QualBench reports MCC and balanced accuracy as primary measures, with sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, Cohen's kappa, Gwet's AC1, and prevalence-and bias-adjusted kappa, and the same measures for two rules that read nothing (every code present and every code absent).
It repeats these at the level of parent codes, checks whether each quotation can be found in its document, measures agreement between repeat runs, and reports cost and time.
Screening runner.

The screening runner expands a declared multiverse into one locked QualFrame configuration per run, validates every configuration without calling an API, records the software version and commit of each run, and enforces study-level and per-run spending limits.
It reserved the worst-case cost of each request against the study limit (US$25) and the per-run limit before sending it, and recorded the cost reported by the provider afterwards.
Each run records its software version and commit, and the final screening commit was 595c937, on a development branch of QualFrame 0.11.0.
Instructions and codebook division.
Both instruction packages require each quotation to be copied exactly from the report and to occur only once in it.

For each package, one paraphrase was drafted with AI assistance and approved by me before any run; it kept the rules, the output format, and the list of codes, but changed the wording and the order of sentences.
The five-part division assigned whole taxonomy groups to parts (four of 19 BCTs and one of 18), and each part was sent with the full report in a separate request.
Runs with the whole codebook made 40 requests and runs with five parts made 200.
The recorded spend of US$13.66 compares with a pre-study estimate of about US$11.

Two calibration runs, cell 15 for each model (decide every code, five parts, high effort), were executed first to check the cost model; they cost more than estimated (US$0.81 against US$0.60 for Haiku and US$0.65 against US$0.33 for Luna) but remained within the limits.
The remaining runs followed in a random order, so that the time of a run was not confounded with any factor.
The per-run spending limit was raised from US$2 to US$3, with my approval, for three Haiku runs with the codebook in five parts.
Runs interrupted by connection errors were resumed from their saved state under a bounded resume policy (13 resumes in total) without repeating completed requests.

The worst-case reservations for the 13 interrupted requests (US$6.71 in total) remain on the ledger because the provider charges for those attempts are unknown; the recorded spend of US$13.66 excludes them.

Output compliance was summarized as the share of quoted passages that could not be located in the report, the number of code labels outside the codebook, and the number of required decisions missing under 'decide every code' (under 'find passages', codes that were not selected are expected to be absent from the output).
Cost per run was the API spend recorded in the budget ledger.
Prospective design declaration.
The screening design, report sample, prompts, and analysis plan were declared in a configuration file and frozen before any screening call.
The declaration was not publicly registered; it is available in the OSF project (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/9287H).
